title: Design the risk out: crates, pallets, pallet jacks and fridge bodies without the sprains and strains
prepared_by: Monaro Milk safety (weekly toolbox talk), from Norco's November 2026 WHS toolbox passed on by Mick Johnson
summary: This week's talk is built on Norco's November 2026 Safety Toolbox, which Mick Johnson passed on. Norco is one of our suppliers, and we are using all of it with thanks. Norco's main message is "Manual Handling – Design the Risk Out: Move smart. Speak up. Prevent injury." Don't just lift differently. Make the task safer. We have checked that message against Safe Work Australia's Hazardous Manual Tasks Code of Practice and SafeWork NSW, and applied it to our own work: crates of bottled milk, pallets, pallet jacks, docks and refrigerated HR trucks and semis. We also cover Norco's Movember and International Men's Day (Thursday 19 November) pages and their wellbeing page on social inclusion.
key_risk: Sprains, strains, back and shoulder injuries and other musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) from hazardous manual tasks at the dock and in the fridge body. These include pushing and pulling loaded pallet jacks, lifting and restacking crates of bottled milk, reaching and twisting to get crates off a pallet, and working bent over or in bulky cold-weather gear in a cold, sometimes wet fridge body. Safe Work Australia and SafeWork NSW say a manual task is hazardous when it involves repetitive or sustained force, high or sudden force, repetitive movement, sustained or awkward posture, or vibration. Injuries can build up slowly through wear and tear, or happen suddenly, for example when a load moves or shifts without warning. Lifting differently does not fix the task. The risk has to be designed out.
drivers_need_to_know: Manual handling is more than lifting. Norco's toolbox and SafeWork NSW both say it includes pushing, pulling, carrying, holding and restraining, plus repetitive movement and awkward or sustained positions. For us that means walking a loaded pallet jack up a dock plate, pulling a pallet to the back of a fridge body, handballing crates off a pallet at a customer, restacking a pallet that has moved, and leaning in to reach the last crates at the front of the body.

Five risk factors make a manual task hazardous (Safe Work Australia Code of Practice; SafeWork NSW; Norco): repetitive or sustained force, high or sudden force, repetitive movement, sustained or awkward posture, and vibration. SafeWork NSW gives a guide: "repetitive" means more than twice a minute, and "sustained" means holding the same position for more than 30 seconds at a time. A task needs more care when it feels physically demanding, needs two people or a stronger person, or needs two hands when it would normally take one. When several risk factors come together, the risk goes up a lot.

Norco's main message: "DON'T JUST LIFT DIFFERENTLY. MAKE THE TASK SAFER." SafeWork NSW says the same thing, that "how to lift" training on its own is not an effective way to protect workers. Before you start a task, ask Norco's five questions.

1. Can the task be eliminated? Is there a way to avoid moving or handling the item at all? For example, deliver the whole pallet to the point of use instead of handballing crates, or skip double handling at the dock. Safe Work Australia lists "deliver goods directly to the point of use to eliminate multiple handling" as an elimination control.

2. Can the task be redesigned? Can the load, equipment, layout, height, distance or process change? For example, build pallets so heavy crates sit at a comfortable height, keep the pallet close so you don't have to reach, cut down on carrying distances, and keep dock floors clear.

3. Is mechanical help available? Use pallet jacks, trolleys, dock levellers, tail lifts (where fitted), and forklifts if you are licensed and authorised. Safe Work Australia lists forklifts, pallet trucks, dock levellers and lift trolleys as mechanical aids. It says aids must be rated for the load, suited to the environment, kept close by, maintained so the effort stays as low as possible, and come with instruction. Pushing a load is better than pulling it: you use your body weight, your lower back does less work and you can see where you are going. Electric pallet jacks cut the effort it takes to get a load moving.

4. Can the exposure be reduced? Cut down on repetition, excessive force, reaching, twisting and long periods in one posture. Swap tasks with a workmate, take micro-breaks on long handballing jobs, and don't save the heaviest work for the end of a long run.

5. Are the controls working? Check the equipment is there, suitable, maintained and being used properly. A pallet jack with flat-spotted or seized wheels, a dock plate that sits proud, or a jack that won't lower properly makes every push harder. Report it, don't put up with it.

Cold and wet make it harder. Safe Work Australia's Code says cold places such as cool rooms and cold stores lower body and hand temperature, which makes gripping harder. Gloves and cold hands make you grip harder. Thick cold-weather clothing restricts movement and can raise the risk of an MSD. Wet or damp items need more force to handle, and they can slip and put a sudden load on your body. Slippery or uneven floors add effort. Inside a refrigerated body, keep gloves dry, wipe away condensation where you can, and take the time to get a proper grip.

Listen to your body (Norco): "Pain and discomfort are warning signs, not part of the job." If you feel pain, discomfort, tingling, numbness, weakness or unusual fatigue: STOP, MAKE THE TASK SAFE, REPORT IT EARLY. Talk to your Monaro Milk supervisor before you carry on. Reporting early gives us the best chance to review the task, get you the right support and stop it turning into something more serious. Safe Work Australia says the same: report problems and signs of discomfort straight away so the risk can be managed before an injury happens.

You know the job best. Norco's toolbox says: "Talk to the people doing the task. They often know where the problems are." SafeWork NSW says the business must consult the workers who do the task, and suggests asking: What makes you sore at work? When do you feel discomfort? What jobs do you avoid doing? Tell us your answers.

Norco's stats (Norco's figures, NOT Monaro Milk's). The front page of Norco's November 2026 toolbox shows "CHECK OUT THE STATS!": LTIFR 3.43, TRIFR 17.3, HAZARDS 47, MSW 35. The PDF does not give a time period, how the figures were worked out, or what the acronyms mean. LTIFR and TRIFR usually stand for Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate and Total Recordable Injury Frequency Rate. MSW is not explained. They are shown here only because they are part of Norco's toolbox. They are not Monaro Milk results and should not be compared with ours.

Norco's Manual Handling Risk Review. Norco's toolbox asks its people to "click here or scan the QR code to access the November Risk Review. Please ensure this is completed by 30 November." The link in Norco's PDF goes to a Norco Microsoft Form: https://forms.cloud.microsoft/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=032aPvefZ0Wmz4IqqKEEanUW-tZEWeFHlAws1BFJ575UOVFXTlFYWDY3SERJU1FVN1BXQk1DUkNEUS4u. It is Norco's form for Norco's review. Monaro Milk staff should only fill it in if your supervisor says so. Monaro Milk will run its own review of our dock and fridge-truck manual tasks (see follow-up actions).

Movember (Norco's page). This Movember, Norco is raising awareness and funds for men's health, including mental health and suicide prevention, prostate cancer and testicular cancer. This month, make a point to: check in with a mate ("How are you really going?"), take the time to listen to the answer, speak up if something doesn't feel right, and make time to look after your own health and wellbeing. Norco's poster also invites people to join its team, Norco Mo Bros & Co, to grow a mo (or a Norco chocolate milk "milk mo"), and to enter Norco's Mo Selfie competition for a chance to win a $50 VISA gift card and the title of Mo Master. That is Norco's campaign and competition, run through QR codes on Norco's poster. It is not a Monaro Milk competition.

International Men's Day, Thursday 19 November (Norco's page, "Making a Difference for Men and Boys", www.internationalmensday.com): take a moment to recognise the positive contributions of the men in our workplaces, families and communities, and encourage conversations about health and wellbeing. On early starts and long runs it is easy to go quiet, so check in with each other this week.

Wellbeing space: social inclusion (Norco's page). "Everyone belongs. Everyone matters." Social inclusion means creating a workplace where everyone feels respected, valued, supported and able to take part, whatever their background, abilities or circumstances. Why it matters at work: psychological safety (people feel safer to speak up and ask for help, which includes reporting a sore back early), stronger teams (trust, connection and cooperation), respect and wellbeing (dignity and fair treatment) and better communication (hearing and valuing different views). Norco's six simple ways to make a difference: INVITE (include others), LISTEN (hear different views), INCLUDE (make space for all), SUPPORT (offer a hand), RESPECT (value differences), SPEAK UP (challenge exclusion). "Small actions create a workplace where everyone belongs."
supervisors_must_check: Pallet jacks (manual and electric), trolleys, dock plates and levellers, and tail lifts where fitted are available where the work happens, rated for a full pallet of bottled milk, and in good order: wheels turning freely, hydraulics holding and lowering, handles and brakes working. Anything faulty is tagged out and reported. Safe Work Australia expects mechanical aids to be maintained so the effort to use them stays as low as possible.

Look for tasks where crates are handballed or a pallet is double handled when it could be delivered whole, built differently or moved mechanically. Start at the top of the hierarchy of control: elimination first, then substitution and engineering (aids, layout, heights), then administrative controls (rotation, workflow). PPE comes last. SafeWork NSW says "how to lift" training on its own is not an effective control.

Talk to the drivers and dock staff who do the tasks (SafeWork NSW says this is required). Ask: What makes you sore? When do you feel discomfort? What jobs do you avoid? Record the answers and the tasks that come up.

Customer drops: list the sites where drivers have to handball crates, push jacks up ramps or over rough or sloping ground, or work without a dock or leveller, and what aid or change could fix each one.

Fridge bodies and the dock: floors are free of ice, condensation, broken crates and debris. Lighting is good enough. Drivers have dry gloves and cold-weather gear that doesn't stop them moving or gripping properly.
Runs and rosters do not stack the heaviest manual handling at the end of a long shift, and tasks are rotated where practicable.

Anyone who reports pain, tingling, numbness, weakness or unusual fatigue is listened to, the task is stopped and made safe before work continues, and an incident or hazard report is completed. Nobody is made to feel they should push on.
Only licensed and authorised people use forklifts.
Everyone who attended has signed on in the Monaro Milk TB Talk app. Norco's own paper Toolbox Talk Record (page 5 of their PDF) is not used for our sign-on.
discussion_questions: Which crate, pallet or pallet-jack task at our dock or at a customer still feels awkward or heavy, especially at the end of a long run? What would make it safer?
Using Norco's five questions, which handballing job could we cut out altogether, redesign, or do with a pallet jack, trolley, leveller or tail lift instead?
Is there a pallet jack, dock plate or other piece of gear right now that is harder to push or use than it should be? Who have you told?
If you felt tingling, numbness or a twinge in your back halfway through a run, what would you do, and who would you call?
Norco's wellbeing question: What can we do as a team to ensure nobody feels left out?
practical_checklist: Before handling: can this be avoided, redesigned or done with a pallet jack, trolley, leveller or tail lift?
Pallet jack checked: wheels roll freely, hydraulics lift, hold and lower, handle and brake OK
Push the jack or trolley rather than pull wherever possible, and keep the path clear
Dock plate or leveller seated properly, and floor in the fridge body and at the dock clear of ice, water and broken crates
Pallet close, heavy crates at a comfortable height, no long reaching or twisting
Dry gloves and cold gear that lets you move and grip properly
Swap tasks or take a short break on long handballing jobs
Forklift only if licensed and authorised
Any pain, tingling, numbness, weakness or unusual fatigue: STOP, make the task safe, report it early to your supervisor
Faulty gear tagged out and reported, not worked around
Checked in with a mate this week (Movember, International Men's Day Thursday 19 November)
required_records: Toolbox talk sign-on for this talk in the Monaro Milk TB Talk app (CSV export or printed register). Norco's paper Toolbox Talk Record (form WHS-FRM-3.03-01.02, February 2024, page 5 of their PDF) is noted but not used. We sign on in the app.
Hazard and incident reports, including early reports of pain or discomfort from manual tasks, and what was done about each.
Monaro Milk hazardous manual task review for dock, customer-drop and fridge-body tasks, recording the task, risk factors, controls chosen (using the hierarchy of control) and review date.
Maintenance and fault records for pallet jacks, trolleys, dock plates and levellers, tail lifts and forklifts.
Forklift licence and authorisation records for anyone who operates a forklift.
Training and instruction records for mechanical aids and manual task risks.

follow_up_actions.action: Run a Monaro Milk hazardous manual task review of dock, customer-drop and fridge-body tasks with the drivers and dock staff who do them, using SafeWork NSW's questions (What makes you sore? When? What jobs do you avoid?) and the hierarchy of control.
Inspect every pallet jack, trolley, dock plate or leveller and tail lift. Tag out and repair or replace anything hard to push, slow to lower or damaged.
List customer drops that involve handballing crates or pushing jacks over ramps or rough ground, and raise changes with each customer (whole-pallet delivery, leveller, better access).
Confirm whether any Monaro Milk staff should complete Norco's November Manual Handling Risk Review form (due 30 November), or whether we only run our own review.
Confirm drivers have suitable dry gloves and cold-weather gear for fridge-body work that still allows grip and movement.
Follow up any sore spots, faulty gear or awkward tasks raised in this talk, and thank Mick and Norco for the toolbox material.
